title: The Forest of Tataka
captions: Beside the Sarayu river, Vishvamitra taught the princes two sacred mantras, Bala and Atibala. With them, they would never feel tired or hungry.
Next they crossed the great river Ganga by boat. From the dark forest ahead came a terrible roar that echoed over the water.
“This land was once green and happy,” said the sage. “Now the rakshasi Tataka lives here. She has the strength of a thousand elephants, and the people have fled.”
“Rama, end her terror and protect the people,” said Vishvamitra. Rama paused, for he had been taught never to harm a woman. “Protecting the helpless is a prince's dharma,” said the sage.
Rama remembered his father's words: obey the sage. He bowed and said, “I will do as you say, for the good of all.” Then he twanged his bowstring with a mighty sound.
Tataka rushed out, raising a storm of dust and hurling rocks. Rama's arrows turned the rocks aside, and with one true arrow the mighty rakshasi fell.
The forest grew calm and bright again. The gods rejoiced, and Vishvamitra blessed Rama with great joy. That night the princes rested peacefully in the forest.
story: Vishvamitra, Rama and Lakshmana walked out of Ayodhya and along the river Sarayu. On its bank the sage taught the princes two sacred mantras called Bala and Atibala. With these mantras, the brothers would never feel tired or hungry on their journey.
Soon they crossed the great river Ganga by boat. As they reached the far bank, a terrible roar echoed out of a dark forest. The trees were thick and silent, and no birds sang.

Vishvamitra explained that this land had once been green and happy, full of villages and farms. Now a rakshasi named Tataka lived there. She had the strength of a thousand elephants, and the people had run away in fear.

The sage asked Rama to end her terror. Rama paused, because he had been taught never to harm a woman. Vishvamitra explained that protecting the helpless is a prince's dharma, and Rama remembered his father's words: obey the sage. He bowed, lifted his bow and twanged the string with a mighty sound.

Tataka rushed out in a storm of dust, hurling rocks. Rama's arrows turned the rocks aside, and with one true arrow the rakshasi fell. The forest grew calm and bright again. The devas rejoiced, and the travellers rested peacefully that night.
value_meaning: doing what is right, protecting the helpless
lesson: Rama did not want to hurt anyone, and he thought carefully before he acted. But Tataka was frightening a whole land, and its people could not protect themselves. Our elders teach that dharma means doing what is right, and standing up for those who cannot protect themselves is right. Rama listened to his teacher and bravely did his duty for the good of all.
lesson_long: Dharma is one of the most important words in our tradition. It means doing what is right, keeping goodness and order in the world, and doing our own duty well.

Rama did not want to hurt anyone. He paused and thought carefully, which shows how gentle his heart was. But a whole land was suffering, and its people could not protect themselves. When his teacher explained his duty, Rama acted bravely for the good of all.
Our elders teach that dharma is not about being strong. It is about using whatever strength we have to protect those who need help.
tradition: Hindu dharma is also called Sanatana Dharma, the eternal way. In the Bhagavad Gita, Lord Krishna says that whenever dharma grows weak, he comes into the world to protect the good and set things right. Rama is honoured as one of these avatars of Lord Vishnu.
In the epics, a rakshasa is a powerful being who brings fear and harm to others, and a rakshasi is a female rakshasa. In the stories they stand for the darkness that dharma must overcome.
words: a female rakshasa, a frightening being in the epics
a form in which God comes into the world
question: Have you ever stood up for someone who needed help? Why was it the right thing to do?
questions: Have you ever stood up for someone who needed help? Why was it the right thing to do?
Rama stopped and thought before he acted. Why is it good to think first?
Who are the people in your life who protect you?
card_lesson: Rama thought carefully, listened to his teacher, and then bravely protected people who could not protect themselves. That is dharma: doing what is right.
